solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Brothers do scream after being shaken up

indicators.note: anything shaken up comes out jumbled, so the letters of DO SCREAM land in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone yells after a nasty jolt, and their siblings join in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brothers' here is comrades-in-arms or union brothers, not siblings; the family picture of the surface is the disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: Brothers in the sense of fellow members of a union or cause, the way activists address one another, are comrades.

clue.text: A method overlooked by actors in Hanks film

indicators.note: to overlook is literally to look down on from above

parts.note: the actors in a production are its cast
a way of doing something is a method

explanation.surface: A technique that the cast of a Tom Hanks movie failed to notice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Overlooked' suggests ignored, but in a down entry it is literal: CAST stands above A WAY.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Cast Away (2000) is the film in which Tom Hanks plays a man stranded on an island.

clue.text: Cap that one might see on Mason?

definitions.meaning: the flat square-topped academic hat worn at graduations

definitions.text: that one might see on Mason
definitions.meaning: a stonemason holds mortar on a square hand-held board

explanation.surface: A hat worn by someone called Mason, perhaps at a graduation.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital M makes Mason look like a name; it is a stonemason, whose board for mortar gave the academic cap its name.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses: the academic cap is named for its likeness to the plasterer's and mason's flat board for holding mortar.

clue.text: Group of stars named road A Different Way

indicators.note: arranging the letters of NAMED ROAD a different way spells a new word

explanation.surface: A constellation has been given the name of a road called A Different Way.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals make 'A Different Way' look like a street name, which hides that it tells you to rearrange NAMED ROAD.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: this northern constellation, named after the chained princess of Greek myth, is one group of stars.

clue.text: Soldiers with energy to get up — that's strange!

indicators.note: in a down entry, getting up means rising from the bottom

explanation.surface: Troops summon the energy to rise, and someone remarks how odd that is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That's' is i.e. read as 'that is', tacked on after the reversed RE plus E.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym with a shade: eerie is strange in a spooky, unsettling way.

clue.text: As might be a Banksy work found on a fence?

definitions.text: As might be a Banksy work found on a fence?

parts.words: As might be a Banksy work
parts.note: Banksy is the anonymous street artist whose works are spray-painted on walls and fences
a fence is also slang for a criminal who receives and sells on goods taken by thieves

explanation.surface: A Banksy mural spotted painted on a garden fence.
explanation.walkthrough: Banksy really does paint on walls and fences, but a fence is also a receiver of stolen goods, so a Banksy found with one has been taken.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads as a description: anything in a fence's hands has been nicked, so the work is stolen.

clue.text: Blow horn on front of Harley-Davidson chopper

indicators.note: in a down entry, one piece on another sits above it

parts.note: to blow a horn is to toot

indicators.note: the front of a word is where its first letter stands

explanation.surface: Sounding the horn on a Harley-Davidson chopper motorbike.
explanation.walkthrough: A chopper is a customised motorbike, which fits a Harley perfectly; here it is the informal word for a tooth.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal British usage: 'choppers' are teeth, so a single chopper is a tooth.

clue.text: Boy seen climbing in valley for the most part

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing means reading from the bottom upward
most of a word but not all of it: its last letter is dropped

parts.note: DALE, a valley, without its last letter

explanation.surface: A boy spotted hiking up through most of a valley.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Valley' is not the word to cut; it gives DALE first, and that is what loses its end.
explanation.definitionFit: An everyday informal synonym: a lad is a boy or young man, especially in British speech.

clue.text: Note a filthy place is not very nice at all

parts.note: a pigsty, a byword for filth

explanation.surface: A remark that some grimy spot is thoroughly unpleasant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Note' is the abbreviation N, not a musical note A to G.
explanation.definitionFit: A phrase definition by understatement: something nasty is far worse than merely not nice.

clue.text: A small pamphlet about British school of art?

parts.note: a tract is a short pamphlet

explanation.surface: A little booklet about a British school of art.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a definition by example: abstract is one school of art among many.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: abstract art, which avoids depicting real objects, is one movement or school in modern painting.

clue.text: One walking fast in street next to jockey

indicators.note: one piece is set right beside the other

explanation.surface: A pedestrian hurrying down a street beside a jockey.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' links the definition to the wordplay; the street does not contain anything.
explanation.definitionFit: An agent noun: to stride is to walk with long, fast steps, so a strider is one who does it.

clue.text: We are fairly shocked!

parts.note: not 'quite' but 'in a fair way': fair-haired
not startled but having a shock, a thick mass of hair

explanation.surface: A group admitting they are quite surprised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fairly' reads as 'quite' but means with fair hair, and 'shocked' means having a shock of hair; so the speakers are fair-haired people.
explanation.definitionFit: Read literally, people with shocks of fair hair are blondes.

clue.text: What Archimedes had man at home put in order

indicators.note: to put things in order is to rearrange them, so the letters of MAN AT HOME are re-sorted

explanation.surface: Archimedes tidying his house.
explanation.walkthrough: Archimedes is said to have cried 'Eureka!' in his bath on grasping displacement, the classic moment of sudden insight.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Archimedes' Eureka in the bath is the textbook sudden flash of insight.

clue.text: Husband with money ultimately is useful

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so take the final letter of money

explanation.surface: A husband who brings in money turns out to be convenient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With' looks like a joining word but supplies AND.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a handy tool is a useful one, convenient to have to hand.

clue.text: Friendly lavatory supremo is quite attractive

parts.note: loo is British slang for a lavatory
a king is a supreme ruler

explanation.surface: A genial boss in charge of toilets turns out to be handsome.
explanation.walkthrough: The absurd picture of a lavatory supremo hides three plain pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: nice-looking is mild praise for appearance, attractive without being stunning.

clue.text: Wearing ace award is first for Lance Stroll

indicators.note: what is worn is wrapped around

parts.note: MBE, Member of the Order of the British Empire, a British honour

indicators.note: the first letter for the word that follows

explanation.surface: Racing driver Lance Stroll wearing a top award.
explanation.walkthrough: Lance Stroll is a Formula One driver, a strange person to link with strolling; the MBE wraps round the L.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain verb synonym: to amble is to stroll at an easy, unhurried pace.

clue.text: Stalemate is uninspiring and bit of a shock

parts.note: a shock of hair is made up of locks

explanation.surface: A stalemate in a game is dull and a little surprising.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shock' means a mass of hair, so a bit of it is a lock.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym borrowed from chess: stalemate, like deadlock, is a position where neither side can progress.

clue.text: Little drink with a jerk could be exciting

parts.note: a tic is an involuntary jerk

explanation.surface: A quick drink shared with an idiot might liven things up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jerk' reads as an insult for a person; here it is a twitch.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: dramatic events are thrilling and striking, as on a stage.

clue.text: Book-keeper annoyed by a riotous entry?

definitions.text: Book-keeper annoyed by a riotous entry?

parts.note: reads as an accountant, but can mean someone who literally keeps books
reads as a bad line in the ledger, but is a noisy arrival in a place that demands quiet

explanation.surface: An accountant irritated by a rowdy line in the ledger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Book-keeper' suggests an accountant and 'entry' a ledger line; read literally, it is someone keeping books who hates a noisy arrival.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue describes the job: a keeper of lending books who famously shushes anyone bursting in noisily.

clue.text: Wasted teacher and nurse tucking into pint

parts.note: pupils call a female teacher Miss

indicators.note: to tuck into something is to get inside it

explanation.surface: A drunk teacher and nurse getting stuck into a pint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wasted' looks like drunk, which fits the pint; it means squandered.
explanation.definitionFit: The squandering sense: time or money misspent has been wasted, as in a misspent youth.

clue.text: What might cloud one's view of large waterfall

definitions.meaning: a medical condition that makes the eye's lens go cloudy
a big, steep fall of water

explanation.surface: Spray blocking someone's view of a big waterfall.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface runs both meanings together so the waterfall seems to be what is being viewed.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses of one word: the eye condition that clouds the lens, and a great downpour of water.

clue.text: Dish dog knocked over by unclosed container

indicators.note: something knocked over ends up the wrong way round
a container left unclosed has no end on it, so TIN loses its final letter

parts.note: a Labrador; turned round it becomes BAL

explanation.surface: A dog knocks over a food bowl beside an open tin.
explanation.walkthrough: A balti is a curry cooked and served in a metal bowl, a British curry-house staple.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses fit: a balti is a curry dish, named after the bowl-shaped pan it is cooked in.

clue.text: Famous pilot's worse after losing one daughter

indicators.note: once it has lost something, the word is left one letter short

parts.note: D = daughter; one of the two Ds goes

explanation.surface: A renowned airman has gone downhill since a daughter died.
explanation.walkthrough: Douglas Bader was a Second World War RAF fighter ace who flew despite having lost both legs.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Douglas Bader, the legless Battle of Britain ace, is among Britain's best-known pilots.

clue.text: County game?

definitions.meaning: the usual short form of an English county west of London
animals hunted for sport, not a match

explanation.surface: Asking whether some pastime belongs to a county.
explanation.walkthrough: Bucks is the usual short form of Buckinghamshire, an English county west of London. 'Game' is the hunted animals, not a sport.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: Bucks abbreviates Buckinghamshire, and bucks, male deer, are shot as game.

clue.text: Managed, say, to climb a series of mountains

indicators.note: in a down entry, climbing goes upward

parts.note: e.g. = for example, 'say'; climbing it becomes GE

explanation.surface: Someone succeeded in scaling a chain of peaks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' is e.g., standing for 'for example'.
explanation.definitionFit: A geographical term: the Alps or Andes are each a range, a connected chain of peaks.

clue.text: Around Open University, a fresh salmon's odd

indicators.note: a fresh version is newly made, so A SALMON is made over into a new order

parts.note: OU = Open University, the UK distance-learning university

explanation.surface: A fresh salmon at the Open University is a curious sight.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram is built first, then split to take OU inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: anomalous means departing from what is normal or expected, hence odd.

clue.text: Old bloke heading to Ibrox to see foreigner

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its first letter, here the I of Ibrox

explanation.surface: An elderly man travels to Ibrox to watch a foreign player.
explanation.walkthrough: Ibrox is Rangers' football stadium in Glasgow; 'heading to' reads as travel but asks for its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: to a British solver someone from Oman is one kind of foreigner.

clue.text: One worker inebriated primarily on church wine

indicators.note: primarily means in the first place, so inebriated gives just its first letter
in an across entry, what is placed on something comes after it

explanation.surface: A tipsy worker drinking the church's communion wine.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces are read in clue order but the church goes first because the rest is 'on' it.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Chianti, the Tuscan red, is one wine among many.

clue.text: Fish the setter of this crossword had caught

indicators.note: to catch someone's words is to hear them, so what follows is a sound

parts.words: the setter of this crossword had
parts.note: the setter says 'I had', shortened to I'd

explanation.surface: The compiler boasting about a fish they once landed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught' fits fishing so well it hides its job: caught as in heard. The ide is pronounced like I'd.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the ide is a European freshwater fish of the carp family.

clue.text: A function without one drop of Niersteiner's silly

indicators.note: in its old sense of outside
a drop is the tiniest bit, so only the first letter of Niersteiner

explanation.surface: A party without a single drop of German wine is a foolish affair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Without' means outside here, not lacking. Niersteiner is a German white wine from Nierstein on the Rhine.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym with a history: asinine, literally donkey-like, means stupid or silly.

clue.text: Small study about Welsh and English state

parts.note: a den is a private study

explanation.surface: A brief study of Wales and England as a nation.
explanation.walkthrough: The Welsh-English picture suggests Britain; the state is Scandinavian.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: Sweden is one sovereign state, the political sense of state rather than condition.

clue.text: How some crossword setters might clue G-12!

definitions.text: How some crossword setters might clue G-12!

parts.words: How some crossword setters might clue G
parts.note: setters often clue a single letter as the middle of some word; G sits at the centre of a five-letter word for the dark hours
twelve o'clock at night, the hour on the clock

explanation.surface: A remark about how compilers would write a clue.
explanation.walkthrough: Setters use 'midnight' for the letter G, the middle of NIGHT, and 12 is the time midnight, so the one word covers both halves of G-12.
explanation.definitionFit: The one word fits both halves: it is twelve at night, and the mid-letter of night is G.
